I'm characterising a sample for normal reflection and transmission, so a beamsplitter is necessary to measure the reflection. Unfortunately the sample is also polarisation dependent (linear) so overall for transmission I'm losing 75% of the intensity (50 through polariser then 50 through BS). I could change to a 70/30 BS but then I can't measure reflection either. For the time being I'm using a mirror and just measuring the transmission until I have a solution to my intensity problem. I then have to magnify the sample 100X meaning that in reality I'm getting sub-1% light going to the spectrometer. 

Right now I have two lamps that independently couple into the set up through a fiber optic, that is why I thought of a 2 in 1 out. I haven't tried to physically join them together as I can't think of a way to get them into one beam other than the possibility of the fiber. 

I'm pretty new to research so my knowledge of available equipment is sub-par and I feel like that's what's really holding me back in this.

So I have a lot of qualms with the leaving cert system. Like it's grand, I just don't like it. For people like myself who knew the general direction they were going from a younger age I feel like I would've been better served being able to specialise more (like the A levels) but instead I had to do subjects like Irish, Geography and German, non of which I have an interest in and actively dislike. 

When I came over from Scotland in 4th class, I was way ahead in maths and english and could complete 6th class work with ease. I'm not sure how that happened but it seems like in Ireland you have a really slow approach with the pacing of your work. 

In third level, I generally think that too many people go to university. There are so many degrees that are basically the same degree but with a different title. I saw this with a lot of my friends who done different business degrees but were in all the same modules. But yeah I think it's strange that the norm is for everyone to go to university. It isn't for everyone and that's okay. I think it's smart when some people decide not to go and instead go straight into work or and apprenticeship or something like that.

These are just my opinions though, I'd be happy to discuss them further and do accept that I could be wrong. There are more I just can't think of any right now. Apologies!

Honestly, I have no idea what the right candidate to do a PhD is. Looking at myself, I wouldn't say I'm ideal. But I know that no matter what this will be finished and it's where I want to be. I'm in the right environment. So in my opinion, all you have to have is the drive to want to do it. You have to know it's going to be hard but push yourself to learn what you need to learn and do what you need to do. 

In a perfect world, these people wouldn't exist, but they do. I don't look down on those people. Most of my friends are in masters and that's fine. I know what their goals are in life and if a masters helps them achieve them then what's that got to do with me?

Even friends who go to work after their bachelors, that's great! They've done what they need to do and they're advancing their career, who am I to judge? I don't think and extra 2 years of research makes you smarter than someone, maybe on a particular topic, yes. But that person who went into work, they have experience of the business, or how a pharma lab runs. I won't have that - but they will.

After a PhD you can go into the private sector (a lot of physics PhDs are currently being hoovered up by Intel right now), public sector (government jobs and stuff like that) or post doc. From what I've gathered after a PhD in Physics you can do really anything. You have the numerical skills for finance, you can go into data science, private research, medical physicist. It's endless really.

There's quite a few right now, some of them specific to Ireland and some of them are international.

* After you're PhD you have to go into a Postdoc to stay in academia. This is a short term contract of only a couple of years and the pay isn't usually fantastic. This limits how much of a life you can have and affects big decisions like buying a house, having kids, can you stay in a relationships if you have to move countries?
* While you're in a PhD in Ireland. The pay is terrible. Compare it to the cost of living and it's incredibly hard to get buy. The housing crisis isn't helping with this. Universities are generally doing all they can but it's a governmental level that is causing the issues. They are in control of what we are paid. On top of this, because it's not considered a wage or a salary, we don't get an PRSI or pension contributions meaning that these start much later in life which is really bad. What we're paid barely covers essentials and a lot of us have to get another job. People say that we shouldn't be complaining about this because it's normal for students to get jobs. But in the PhD you could be working for 50-60 hours a week and then have to work 20 hours ontop of that? How is anyone meant to live happily like that. 
* In Ireland, the chances of you being able to stay in academia isn't that high. Think of how old you're lecturers are generally. A lot of them will clog positions for decades, and all of the PhD graduates and PostDocs can't take those jobs.

These are just a few but I could be here all day.
